name: Gallon of milk a day (GOMAD)

card.summary: A gallon of whole milk a day for a big calorie surplus; popular in strength circles, untested as a named method.
card.note: No studies of the method; large surpluses add body fat.

quick.overview:
GOMAD means drinking about a gallon of whole milk daily alongside meals to force weight gain. It comes from strength-training communities and is discussed by those wanting to bulk.

No studies of it as a named method were found.
quick.mechanism: Milk adds a large amount of calories and protein, producing a calorie surplus.
quick.risks: Reference material on bulking notes bigger surpluses add more fat. Dairy is a trigger for people with milk allergy or lactose intolerance.

lead: GOMAD, short for 'gallon of milk a day', is a weight-gain method from strength-training communities in which a lifter drinks about a gallon of whole milk daily on top of regular meals. The aim is a large, easy-to-consume calorie and protein surplus to gain size quickly, which lifters pursue to build a bigger, more muscular physique. [1][2]

MEL Magazine describes it as a small trend among bodybuilders and lifters, discussed on forums, and says a gallon of milk adds roughly 2,400 calories. One lifter it profiles traced his version to the 'Squats and Milk' program in the book Super Squats. [1] On T Nation, members tie it to that program: one recalls drinking a gallon a day for six weeks in his early twenties while running Super Squats, and another says to 'drink a gallon of milk a day and squat your face off'. [2][3]

No clinical trial has tested GOMAD as a named method. Users in the MEL piece reported gains of 12 pounds in six weeks and of about 3 pounds a week, and several said much of the weight was fat; they also reported bloating, gas and hard stools. [1]

chain: A gallon of whole milk adds roughly 2,400 calories and protein to the day
Large calorie surplus supports heavy training and weight gain
More total body mass, with muscle gains mixed with fat
angle.text: GOMAD is used to add a large calorie and protein surplus alongside hard training, so that bodyweight and muscle size climb quickly. Users report fast weight gain, much of it fat.

infobox: About 128 oz (one US gallon) of whole milk daily [1]

paras: The method adds a large daily volume of milk, usually whole, to normal eating. MEL Magazine puts the intake at 128 ounces and about 2,400 extra calories. [1] It is most associated with the Super Squats program, whose members on T Nation describe pairing it with heavy squatting. [2][3]

MEL Magazine profiles three men. One went from 160 to 240 pounds over seven months and reached a 1,000-pound powerlifting total, acknowledging much of the gain was fat; another gained 12 pounds in six weeks; a third raised his deadlift from 260 to 345 pounds over two months while gaining about 3 pounds a week, mostly fat. They reported bloating, gas, painful stools and being winded, and most said they would not recommend it to the average person. [1]

On T Nation, a member who planned a Super Squats-style block said he did not intend to drink a gallon a day and thought there were better choices; another noted the sugar content of a gallon of milk made him think carefully about it and mentioned lower-sugar and lactose-free milk options. [4][5] In a thread about college-age mistakes, one reply jokes that the gallon of milk a day is 'a rite of passage'. [6]

Nutritionist Summer Yule, quoted in MEL Magazine, linked high dairy and calcium intake to prostate cancer risk and warned that a gallon of milk puts a person at over twice the tolerable upper intake level of calcium for adults, and that heavy milk drinking can crowd out other nutrients. [1]
No studies found testing GOMAD as a named method.

lore.intro: In T Nation threads GOMAD is discussed as a staple of the Super Squats program and as a rite of passage for young lifters, with some members choosing lower-sugar milk or skipping it. [2][3][5]

claims.claim: A gallon of milk a day on top of heavy squatting reliably adds muscle mass.
claims.believers: Members say following the program with the milk, or with large amounts of eggs and meat, is 'bound to grow' a lifter. [3]
claims.experts: No published trial has tested the method; MEL Magazine's interviewees report that much of the weight gained was fat. [1]

claims.claim: The milk's sugar content makes it a poor fit for some lifters.
claims.believers: A T Nation poster said the sugar in a gallon of milk made him think carefully, and cited a lower-sugar milk option. [5]
claims.experts: Nutritionist Summer Yule cites calcium over the tolerable upper intake level and crowding out of other nutrients as concerns. [1]
